title: Business functions and connected decisions
concept: Marketing defines a customer promise, operations delivers it, finance tests affordability, and people management provides skills and accountability. A decision that improves one department can damage the whole service. Trace an order across functions and specify what information must cross each handoff.
case: Fictional case: sales promises 30 orders today while operations can deliver 20. More advertising does not close this gap. Renegotiate the promise with customers or verify and cost extra capacity. Blaming operators alone hides the coordination failure.
task: Map one order through sales, operations and finance. Record information, owner and handoff time. Identify one conflict, propose two responses, and compare customer, cost and capacity effects.
question: What is needed before promising 30 orders?
correct: Available capacity and existing commitments
wrong: Advertising follower count alone

title: Environment, stakeholders and ethical decisions
concept: Stakeholders affect or are affected by a business. Customers, workers, suppliers and neighbours can have different interests. Separate external conditions from internal capabilities. Ethical analysis considers harm, fairness and honesty alongside revenue. Limited power to complain does not make a stakeholder unimportant.
case: Fictional case: running a machine at night speeds delivery but disturbs neighbours and fatigues workers. Compare scheduling changes, sound insulation and workload redistribution. Compensation does not automatically remove harm or replace checking local requirements.
task: Map five stakeholders, their interests, possible harm and voice in the decision. Design two alternatives, justify a choice and identify missing evidence that could change it.
question: Does limited power to object justify ignoring harm?
correct: No; assess harm and ways to reduce it
wrong: Yes, if revenue increases

title: Reading data and limits of inference
concept: A count answers how many; a rate needs a numerator and denominator; a trend needs comparable periods. Improvement does not establish its cause. Separate observation, calculation and assumption. Record sample size and selection. Do not compare rates with different definitions or periods without explaining the difference.
case: Fictional case: complaints rise from 4 of 40 orders to 6 of 100. The count increases while the rate falls from 10% to 6%. Service may have improved, but reporting methods or customer mix may also have changed.
task: Tabulate both periods and calculate rates. Write one misleading headline and one accurate headline. List three alternative explanations and evidence that distinguishes them. Rewrite your conclusion with its limits.
question: What is the second-period complaint rate?
wrong: 15%, using the first-period denominator

title: Leadership, management and accountability
concept: Management organises resources and follow-up; leadership helps people understand and pursue direction. One person can do both. Task responsibility, decision authority and accountability are related but distinct. Clear roles support collaboration by preventing everyone from waiting for someone else.
case: Fictional case: a launch stalls because a designer awaits the manager, who assumes the coordinator approved it. Motivation alone will not fix ambiguous authority. Specify who authorises publication, who reviews it and when delays escalate.
task: Choose a five-task project. Assign an executor, decision owner and reviewer to each task. Test the arrangement against an absent decision owner and define a fallback that respects sensitive permissions.
question: What should address conflicting approvals first?
correct: Clarify the decision owner and authority
wrong: Send only a motivational message

title: Decision-making and problem-solving
concept: Define the gap between actual and desired performance. Separate symptoms from possible causes and gather evidence before fixing on one explanation. Compare alternatives, including temporarily maintaining the current approach. Set criteria before favouring an option. Reversible decisions can use bounded trials with stop conditions.

question: Does late delivery prove the machine is the cause?

wrong: Yes; delays always mean too few machines

title: Communication, delegation and feedback
concept: Delegation specifies the outcome, deadline, resources, authority and review point. It is not handing over an ambiguous task and judging against unstated expectations. Useful feedback describes observable behaviour and its effect, invites the other person’s explanation and agrees a verifiable next step.

title: Teams, motivation and conflict
concept: Teams need shared goals, roles, information and working agreements. Motivation is not only reward: clarity, fairness and the ability to succeed also matter. title: Negotiating and documenting agreements
concept: Clarify your needs, acceptable limits and alternative if no agreement is reached. Ask about the other party’s needs. Compare price, quality, delivery and payment together; a lower price may cost more after delays. A clear agreement specifies obligations, verification and change handling.

title: Choosing a problem and customer segment
concept: A segment groups customers with similar contexts, needs and purchasing behaviour. “Everyone” does not guide service design or testing. Describe the problem before choosing a solution. title: Customer research and interview questions
concept: Ask about recent experiences, actual behaviour and current alternatives, then clarify reasons or sequence. Leading questions suggest an answer; future enthusiasm is not a purchase. Obtain consent for recording, minimise collected data and avoid generalising a small sample to the entire market.

wrong: Polite enthusiasm for an untried idea

title: Value proposition and business model
concept: A value proposition identifies the customer, problem, useful outcome and reason to choose the offer over alternatives. A business model connects this to activities, resources, partners, channels, revenue and costs. Coherence matters more than filling boxes: fast service needs feasible operations and economics.

wrong: Yes; the resource is always the value

title: Channels, selling and customer experience

title: Pricing and unit economics
concept: Price is not profit. Unit contribution equals price minus variable cost and helps cover fixed costs before producing a positive result. Examine discounts, commissions and rework. This simplified model does not replace full accounting or research into willingness to pay.
case: Fictional case: price 150 and variable cost 90 give contribution 60. A price of 140 gives 50. Matching the contribution from 20 old-price orders needs 24 new-price orders, assuming unchanged costs and sufficient capacity.
task: Compare three prices and unit contributions. Calculate orders needed to cover fictional fixed costs of 900, rounding up where necessary. State limitations and design a willingness-to-pay test.
question: What is contribution at price 140 and variable cost 90?
correct: 50 before fixed costs
wrong: 140 net profit

title: Generating and selecting ideas
concept: Separate generating alternatives from evaluating them. Start with a defined problem and vary service sequence, access or division of work. Evaluate customer benefit, capability, cost and risk. Scores structure discussion but do not turn assumptions into facts.

title: Market, alternatives and competition
concept: A market is not everyone who might hear about an offer. Define segment, location, period and reach, then distinguish estimated demand from sales you can serve. Alternatives include another provider, doing it yourself or postponing. Compare using customer criteria rather than price alone.

title: Operational feasibility and capacity
concept: Capacity is output achievable within a period under defined quality conditions. A bottleneck can constrain a sequential process. Measure processing, waiting and rework separately. Available staff time is not all productive time; consider breakdowns, breaks and differences between orders.
case: Fictional case: checking handles 8 orders per hour, printing 12 and binding 10. In a stable sequential model, the maximum is 8 orders per hour. Speeding printing alone does not raise that limit.

title: Costs, revenue, breakeven and cash flow
concept: For a single-product model, breakeven units equal fixed costs divided by positive unit contribution, under stated assumptions. Accounting profit and cash collection differ. Closing cash equals opening cash plus receipts minus payments; sales alone cannot determine it.
case: Fictional case: fixed costs of 900 and contribution of 60 give breakeven at 15 orders. Opening cash 500, receipts 2,400 and payments 2,700 give closing cash 200. Credit sales may not yet appear in receipts.
task: Build three sales-volume scenarios and a two-week cash schedule. Separate sales, collection and payment dates. Delay a receipt of 600, identify any shortfall and discuss responses without treating a loan as sales revenue.
question: What is closing cash in the example?

title: Testing, scenarios and continuation decisions
concept: Turn a critical assumption into a testable question. Specify a measure, decision threshold, test size and duration before observing results. Scenarios combine consistent assumptions; sensitivity analysis varies a particular factor. A limited test supports a limited decision, not guaranteed success at scale.
case: Fictional case: 8 of 10 collection-slot orders arrive on time against a predeclared threshold of 9. Do not lower the threshold after seeing results. Investigate delays and revise the test before expanding.
task: Write an experiment card with assumption, measure, threshold and actions for success or failure. Add conservative and base scenarios, then justify continue, revise or stop with evidence limitations.
question: How should a missed predeclared threshold be handled?

wrong: Lower it afterwards to declare success

title: Experiment validity and bias
concept: Results can reflect participant selection, seasonality or several simultaneous changes. Record who was included and excluded, and distinguish intervention effects from alternative explanations. Fair allocation and consistent measurement help, but a small sample still has substantial limitations.
case: Fictional case: a discount offered to friends during exam week produces more orders than an ordinary week. Discount, participant relationships and timing all changed. Design a comparison with more similar participants and timing.
task: Audit the previous experiment for three biases. Redesign the comparison, specify constants and changes, and record exclusions. Write a conclusion limited to the tested participants and conditions.
question: Does the increase establish the discount effect alone?

wrong: Yes; every increase after a discount is caused by it

title: Vision, mission and measurable goals

title: Environment, capabilities and priorities

title: Positioning, marketing and sales planning
concept: Positioning defines how a chosen segment should see an offer relative to alternatives. Connect the promise to evidence, a channel and a clear purchase step. title: An integrated business plan and measures

title: Reviewing a plan and its sensitivity
concept: Review the plan as if your favourite assumption were wrong. Vary an influential factor while initially holding others constant, then examine a scenario with related changes. Combining arbitrary worst values does not create a forecast. Distinguish possible events from preventive decisions.

title: Formation requirements and local verification
concept: Formation, licensing and tax requirements vary by jurisdiction, activity and legal form. Do not transfer a checklist between countries as if universally valid. title: Performance monitoring and improvement
concept: Monitoring compares actual performance with a clear baseline and explains variance rather than merely displaying numbers. Activity and outcome measures differ, and improvement can trade off against quality. Test a small change, monitor its effect and a guardrail, then retain, revise or reverse it.
case: Fictional case: average order time falls from 20 to 15 minutes while rework rises from 2 to 8 of 100 orders. Speed alone hides a quality decline. Investigate the changed process steps.
task: Define four metrics with sources and baselines. Analyse a variance and propose an improvement test, guardrail and rollback decision. Write a report separating facts from interpretation.
question: Is shorter time enough to declare improvement?
correct: No; examine quality and rework
wrong: Yes; speed makes other measures irrelevant

title: Acceptance criteria and handover
concept: Implementation completion is not acceptance. Acceptance criteria describe verifiable behaviour or results, judged by an authorised recipient. Handover includes usage, limitations, support ownership and known defects. Record acceptance or rejection against specific evidence.
case: Fictional case: booking works on success but loses data after connection failure. “The form is ready” is insufficient. Recovery or clear user-notification criteria expose what must be fixed before acceptance.
task: Write five acceptance criteria and a test for each. Prepare a handover with version, owner and deferred defects. Conduct a self-review and record missing evidence.
question: What is stronger acceptance evidence?
correct: Test results linked to agreed criteria
wrong: Only the implementer saying it is finished

title: Closing a project and learning from it
concept: Closure confirms acceptance, transfers responsibility and records remaining commitments. A learning review asks what was expected, what happened, why and what will change next time. Avoid blame and generic advice; connect each lesson to evidence, a change and an owner.
case: Fictional case: approval delays recur in three tasks. “We need more cooperation” specifies no action. An alternate approver and escalation time limit create a change testable in the next project.
task: Write a short closure report and three lessons learned. For each, provide evidence, possible cause, action, owner and measure. Separate established facts from explanations requiring verification.
question: Which lesson learned is actionable?
correct: Define an alternate approver and escalation deadline
wrong: A general request for better cooperation

title: Evidence audit and defending a plan
concept: A persuasive plan depends on coherent reasoning and evidence limits, not delivery confidence alone. Classify claims as observations, calculations, assumptions or decisions. Important claims need traceable internal support. Stating uncertainty with a verification plan is stronger than presenting assumptions as facts.
case: Fictional case: five interviews do not establish that all students want a service. Say “the problem appeared in three of five exploratory interviews; a broader test is needed.” Do not hide cases that disagree.
task: Audit ten claims in your plan and classify them. Prepare five challenging questions and answers grounded in evidence or its limits. Correct an overstated claim and define the next test.
question: How should a five-interview finding be stated?
correct: With sample size and generalisation limits
wrong: As a fact about all customers

title: Presenting and reviewing the integrated project
concept: The final project integrates problem, customer, value, business model, feasibility, operations, schedule, risks and metrics. It is not a stack of separate files: assumptions, figures and decisions must agree across sections. Explain your choices, what could change them and a bounded next action.
case: Fictional case: reducing price to 140 should update contribution, breakeven and cash; demand and capacity assumptions may also change. Old tables create contradictions even in an attractive presentation.
task: Submit an integrated plan, one-page summary and five-minute presentation. Check arithmetic, three risks, demand evidence and local-verification limits. Apply the rubric, revise the weakest section and record the change.
question: What must be updated when price changes?
correct: Connected calculations and assumptions throughout
wrong: Only the pricing page title
